text: The chair of the committee or the ranking member? In the committee, the ranking member is just the leader of the minority side of things. And so for the Democrats, that'll be Maxine Waters. She'll be the ranking member. And the. But the chair is the one who really sets the agenda for everything. They are the ones who hire all the committee staff. They are the ones that decide which bills come up for a vote. Oftentimes, the chair will write the bill for that committee. So, for example, in the Armed Services Committee, the chair of that committee is the one who writes the base text of that bill, which is an $800 billion bill. So they have tremendous power in writing that first draft, and obviously other members can amend it and whatnot. But there's a tremendous amount of deference from other committee members to the committee chair and their staff, and similarly. And John can speak to this as well, but from a leadership perspective. So the speaker, the majority leader, the minority leader, they can't be experts on every single topic. And so oftentimes they're going to defer to the committee chair, who's sort of the subject matter expert, has been studying the this, has the hearings, has the committee staff expertise. And oftentimes, if a committee chair and those committee members vote for something and it goes to the floor, the leadership will defer to that and say, we trust your judgment. You've been spending years on this, becoming experts on this. There are times where members of leadership will go in and say, we need this provision or that provision but broadly speaking, the committee chair is the one who creates the policy at the end of the day, working with their committee members. text: Yeah, absolutely. So it is a budget tool where if the House and Senate agree on the Exact same budget resolution. And they also have instructions in that budget resolution. The point of the tool was to reduce the deficit. It has not necessarily done that in recent years. But the cheat code it unlocks is that you only need a 50% plus one vote in the Senate. Typically with the filibuster still intact, you need 60 votes in the Senate. And since neither Republicans or democrats have had 60 members of their party in the majority in quite some time, the minority always has a say. And that then obviously necessitates more horse trading. What reconciliation unlocks is essentially you can do a party line vote, completely shut out the minority party if you so choose, and pass the bill through the House and Senate and to the President's desk. The Senate is, no offense, Gio and I are both House guys, but that is where a lot of bills go to die. It just. The House moves a lot quicker because of the filibuster. The Senate moves much more deliberately and slowly. And we don't need to go into the pros and cons of that. But this is a fast track process. And Republicans have already stated that they want to use that process to primarily again, extend the Trump tax cuts and address other issues in the tax code.
